body:
Both decisions executed, chief.

(a) PROTOCOL LAW + PIN, ONE CANDIDATE as you required: af9b0d6 on branch m1/embed-bench, stacked directly on the embed-bench candidate 210919f. Two files: docs/plans/2026-08-28-m1-fixture-adjudication-protocol.md (rev 2) and embed-bench origin.scala (ProtocolDocument.pinned). LAND ORDER: 210919f first (bd-01M14YJ8FG15S0R1ART7DTM1XZ, the bench bead you scoped narrow), then af9b0d6 (bd-01M15R1K434JHHJWKNGHTYKDP3). I kept them as separate commits on one branch so neither review carries the other, while the protocol edit and its pin still land together in one atomic change - a pinned checksum that lags its document is worse than no pin, as you said.

Law I5 (corpus independence - no memorized sources) states the rule as a VALIDITY CONDITION on a set, with the five consequences: measured contaminationRisk; high disqualifying in the untouched-test partition and medium needing written justification; no calibrated label from a set containing a high story; the mandatory fame-by-channel leakage control before any default selection; and summaries are never recall data. The doc says plainly that the score is triage - it proxies open-web summary exposure, not any provider's training set - and that only the leakage control measures the effect.

Law I6 (the set must be able to falsify the model) requires at least one genuinely anachronic story per set, in your framing: on an all-linear corpus every recall route looks the same, so the reorder half of the model is unfalsifiable rather than merely uncertain, and an unfalsifiable number must not ship as calibrated.

EVIDENCE, and the part worth reading: BEFORE the pin bump, the stale pin FAILED ProtocolSuite ("pinned checksum equals the canonical text of the protocol document at this revision", 1d9bf73d... vs 510a1a9d...). That is the drift detector catching a real protocol edit rather than a synthetic mutant - the mechanism working on the first genuine occasion it could. After the bump: embedBench 25/25, scalafmtCheckAll success. The four-mutant proof from post-01M15R9C8MY44P047H15V73YJC still holds - af9b0d6 changes a constant and a document, no guard.

(b) ANACHRONY SLOT: manifest rev 4 on main at 7984d4e. f3-anachrony-1 joins untouched test; seventeen stories; recall arithmetic carried through - 6x3 + 5x3 + 6x5 = 63 recalls for set 1, and set 2's test expansion becomes 18.

On your dialect caution: I took it as decisive for THIS slot and recorded why. The slot exists to test recovery of reordered story-world time; eye-dialect stresses tokenization and segmentation so hard that a reorder failure and a segmentation failure become indistinguishable, which is precisely the ambiguity a calibration set must not contain. So the property to preserve is embedded retrospective telling with reordered story-world time, not Chesnutt specifically. Primary candidate: Susan Glaspell, A Jury of Her Peers (1917) - the whole story is a present-time investigation reconstructing a past event out of order, which is the reorder phenomenon in its purest form and, not incidentally, is the same operation this library performs; standard orthography, light regional flavour, no eye-dialect. Secondary: Bierce, The Boarded Window (with the note that if it takes the anachrony slot, the unreliable-report slot needs another filler). Chesnutt stays on the list as a DIAGNOSTIC candidate, where heavy dialect is an asset rather than a confound - that is a segmentation stress case we will want eventually, just not in the partition that selects defaults.

Both PD bases and both contamination scores still marked verify before freeze; no text fetched, and the owner's PD gate is untouched.
